body.text: Meitei organizations in the Indian northeastern state of Manipur held a massive rally in Imphal on Saturday demanding protection of indigenous people, abrogation of the Suspension of Operations (SoO) agreement with militant groups, and the resignation of Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh for failing to halt the ethnic strife.

The rally, which was endorsed by the Naga apex body, the United Naga Council, came on the heels of a series of incidents over the past several months in the state. There has been a further escalation of the violence that began more than three years ago in May 2023 between Manipur’s Meitei majority and Kuki-Zo communities. So far, more than 300 people have been killed, and 49 are missing.

Over the past year, communities that were previously untouched by the conflict are getting drawn into the violence. In February, the confrontation between the Naga and Kuki intensified after an altercation at the Litan-Sareikhong area in Manipur’s Ukhrul district. What began supposedly as a local dispute escalated into attacks on homes, abductions, and armed clashes across the districts of Ukhrul, Kamjong, Senapati, and Kangpokpi. Authorities imposed a curfew in the affected areas, and the internet was suspended across Ukhrul.

On May 13, three Kuki church leaders were killed in an ambush in Kangpokpi. On the same day, 18 Naga civilians were abducted, of whom six were killed, and their mutilated bodies were recovered on June 10. Since then, more than 50 people from both communities have been killed.

Naga organizations have accused Kuki-Zo rebel groups that are part of the SoO with the government of being involved in some of these attacks. Kuki organizations have blamed the two Naga outfits – National Socialist Council of Nagalim (Isak Muivah) or NSCN(IM) and Zeliangrong United Front-Kamson (ZUF-K) – for the violence.
Meitei Hindus and Pangal Muslims also clashed last month in Thoubal, resulting in the death of one person. Many houses were set ablaze.

This incident was followed by another on October 19 along the boundary between Imphal East and Kangpokpi districts, when unidentified assailants opened fire on a group of Meitei woodcutters. Three people were killed and another three were injured. Three people have so far been arrested for their alleged involvement in the killings.
The killings sparked protests in the state capital, Imphal, as enraged residents placed two dead bodies outside the chief minister’s residence and demanded arrest of the killers.

At the heart of the multilayered strife in Manipur are historical grievances, lopsided land laws, uneven distribution of resources, and political marginalization. The demand for Scheduled Tribe status by the majority Meiteis, which was the immediate cause of the unrest on May 3, 2023, has long been an issue of debate as ST status would grant them rights enjoyed by tribal communities like the Kuki-Zo and Naga.

Many of these issues and conflicts can be traced to the colonial period. After India’s independence in 1947, the issues were not addressed. The grievances festered, prompting radical sections from all the communities to form rebel groups for redressal of their grievances and other objectives.

Beginning in the late 1990s, the government signed a series of ceasefire agreements with rebel groups from the Naga and Kuki-Zo communities. Most of the key demands by these organizations, such as the creation of homelands, were rejected by the government. The ceasefires were repeatedly extended by the government without any specific roadmaps.

However, in a reversal of its earlier policy, the government did not renew the agreements with the 25 Kuki-Zo groups following their expiry in September 2026. The reason could have been the killing of three Meitei civilians on October 19 and the subsequent reactions from Naga and Meitei civil society groups. Besides, in August, nine Naga legislators had made a case before Home Minister Amit Shah to abrogate the agreements.

The government’s response to the crisis in Manipur leaves much to be desired. President’s rule was invoked in Manipur in February last year, and lifted a year later. A new chief minister was sworn in with two deputy chief ministers belonging to the Kuki and Naga communities. But that has hardly helped to de-escalate the tense situation in the state.

The government has increased the deployment of security forces in Manipur. Recent reports claim that more troops are likely to be diverted from anti-Maoist operations in Chhattisgarh to Manipur. While controlling the ethnic strife certainly necessitates a greater presence of security forces, the path to peace in Manipur requires more than stepping up the deployment security forces in the state. An approach that includes dialogue between the warring communities and redressal of long-standing grievances and cross-border issues is important.
